record.paper_title: Advances in periodic difference equations with open problems
record.original_question: For a continuous interval map f, let D(f) denote its collection of dynamical properties, and call a property P an L-property if P is preserved when f is restricted to a compact subinterval and linearly rescaled back to [0, 1] in the sense described in the paper. Given three L-properties P1, P2, and P3, prove or disprove that there exist commuting maps f0, f1: [0, 1] → [0, 1] such that f0 has property P1, f1 has property P2, and the composition f0 ∘ f1 has property P3.

evidence.quote: For a map f ∈ C(I), I = [0, 1], denote by D(f) the set of dynamic properties of f ... A dynamic property P ∈ D(f) is an L–property if for any continuous map f and any compact subinterval J ⊆ [0, 1], it is held that P ∈ D(f) ∩ D(fJ ).
Theorem 6.1. Let Pi, i = 1, 2, 3, be L–properties. Then there are f0, f1 ∈ C(I) such that P1 ∈ D(f0), P2 ∈ D(f1) and P3 ∈ D(f0 ◦ f1).
Open Problem 6.1. State an analogous result to Theorem 6.1 when the maps f0 and f1 commute.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $I = [0,1]$ and let $C(I)$ denote the set of continuous self-maps of $I$. For $f \in C(I)$, let $D(f)$ denote the collection of dynamical properties of $f$ (e.g., positive topological entropy, Li–Yorke chaos, existence of periodic points of given periods, transitivity, etc.).

Given a compact subinterval $J \subseteq I$ that is invariant under $f$ (i.e., $f(J) \subseteq J$), let $f_J \in C(I)$ denote the map obtained by restricting $f$ to $J$ and conjugating by the unique increasing affine bijection from $J$ onto $[0,1]$, so $f_J : [0,1] \to [0,1]$ is the natural rescaling of $f|_J$.

Call a dynamical property $P$ an $L$-property if, for every $f \in C(I)$ and every compact invariant subinterval $J \subseteq I$, one has $P \in D(f)$ whenever $P \in D(f_J)$ (that is, the property lifts from rescaled invariant subintervals to the full map).

It is known that for any three $L$-properties $P_1, P_2, P_3$ there exist maps $f_0, f_1 \in C(I)$ such that $P_1 \in D(f_0)$, $P_2 \in D(f_1)$ and $P_3 \in D(f_0 \circ f_1)$.

Question: Prove or disprove that, for any three $L$-properties $P_1, P_2, P_3$, the maps $f_0$ and $f_1$ above can be chosen to additionally commute, i.e., $f_0 \circ f_1 = f_1 \circ f_0$, with $P_1 \in D(f_0)$, $P_2 \in D(f_1)$, and $P_3 \in D(f_0 \circ f_1)$.
artifact.status_search_result: A web search did not return any specific resolution of the commuting-maps version of the Parrondo-type combination theorem for L-properties of continuous interval maps. Surveys on dynamic Parrondo's paradox indicate the area remains active with several open questions, but no published proof or disproof of this specific commuting variant was located.

status_evidence.title: Chaos and Parrondo's paradox: An overview
status_evidence.snippet: The literature on dynamic Parrondo's paradox has been rather sparse although many interesting questions remain open, from both the mathematical and physical viewpoints.
status_evidence.claim: Open questions remain in dynamic Parrondo's paradox for interval maps.

status_evidence.title: Parrondo's Paradox for Tent Maps
status_evidence.snippet: Constructive procedure for obtaining Parrondian dynamics combining interval maps.
status_evidence.claim: Constructions of Parrondian dynamics for interval maps are studied, but the commuting case is not addressed in this work.
